scenario: AITA for telling people there is no end credit scene? | IF YOU CARE ABOUT END CREDIT SCENES LIKE THESE PEOPLE DONT READ I GUESS So, I have been working at a movie theater for a summer job, and my movie theater has ushers, but ushers at our theater don’t rip people’s tickets, they just clean the theaters. So that’s what I’ve been doing recently on my shifts and it’s pretty laid back and easy. So ushers get a door sheet, and it has what theaters to go to in an order so you can clean each theater after everyone gets out efficiently. And I had Dark Phoenix and another movie to clean at the same time. It’s super slow on weekdays so it’s not a big deal. But I knew the other movie besides Dark Phoenix was pretty crowded so I wanted to be as efficient as possible. So when I walked into Dark Phoenix, and the credits were rolling, there was 4 sets of people still in the theater presumably waiting for the end credit scene like most super hero movies have these days. So, to help them out (in my mind I guess) and myself out to clean the theater faster, I told them “hey guys, you don’t have to wait around there’s no end credit scene.” I’ve done this many times with no issues but this couple in this showing had an issue. They got up from their seat and yelled at me for “ruining their movie going experience” and wanted to speak to a manager. So I call a manger to the theater and they tell the manger that I was rude for spoiling that there was no end credit scene and they complained also that I was shining a flash light as well. I told my manager that last part was false but I didn’t see an issue with telling them as it saved them time. My manager told the couple we were sorry and he gave them a free movie pass. Once they left, my manager told me to just stop telling people about how there’s no end credit scene. So Reddit, AITA for telling people there’s no end credit scene or was this just a weird couple?

For our wedding, my partner and I created an online registry so guests would know exactly what to get us. My mother thinks it's rude to tell people what to buy. Would you still use the registry?

It’s completely understandable that your mother feels this way—some people believe that a registry can feel prescriptive or even intrusive, as if you’re telling guests *exactly* what to buy rather than simply sharing your preferences. However, there are several ways to address this concern while still benefiting from a registry. Here are some suggestions: ### 1. **Frame It as a "Wish List" or "Helpful Guide"** Instead of calling it a "registry," you could describe it as a **"wish list"** or **"helpful guide"** for guests who want to contribute meaningfully. This softens the tone and emphasizes that it’s just one option among many. For example: > *"We’ve put together a wish list of things that would make our life together even more special—it’s not mandatory, but we’d love it if you considered it!"* ### 2. **Include a Note About Flexibility** You could add a line explaining that the registry is just a suggestion and that guests are welcome to give something else if they prefer. This reassures them that they’re not being told what to buy. For example: > *"We’ve included a registry for your convenience, but we’d be just as grateful for any thoughtful gift that reflects your relationship with us!"* ### 3. **Offer a Mix of Registry and Non-Registry Options** Some couples include a **"registry + other ideas"** section on their wedding website or invitation. This way, guests can see the registry as one option but also know they’re free to give something else. For example: > *"We’ve included a registry for your convenience, but we’d love any gift that brings you joy—whether it’s from our registry or not!"* ### 4. **Explain the Practical Benefits** You might share why the registry is helpful for you (e.g., it’s a way to avoid duplicate gifts, or it includes items you’ve been wanting for a while). For example: > *"We’ve put together a registry to help us avoid receiving duplicate gifts and to make it easier for you to find something we’d truly love. But we’d be just as happy with a gift that’s special to you!"* ### 5. **Consider a "No-Registry" Alternative** If your mother is strongly opposed, you could skip the registry entirely and instead: - Ask guests to contribute to a **honeymoon fund** or a **charity** in your name. - Encourage them to give **experiences** (e.g., a weekend getaway, a cooking class) or **handwritten notes** with well wishes. - Provide a **list of local businesses** you love (e.g., restaurants, bookstores) where guests can give gift cards. ### 6. **Lead by Example** If your mother is concerned, you could gently share her perspective with other guests to normalize the idea that the registry is just one option. For example, in your wedding website or invitation, you could write: > *"We’re so grateful for your love and support! Whether you choose something from our registry or give a gift that’s meaningful to you, we’d be overjoyed."* ### Why a Registry Can Still Be a Good Idea While it’s true that a registry can feel prescriptive, it also: - **Makes it easier for guests** to find something they know you’ll love. - **Avoids duplicate gifts** (which can be frustrating for couples). - **Helps you plan** for things you’ve been wanting (e.g., kitchen gadgets, travel gear). - **Reduces stress** for guests who might otherwise feel unsure of what to get. ### Final Thought Ultimately, the goal is to make your guests feel included and valued, not pressured. If your mother’s concern is about feeling like you’re dictating their choices, you can reassure her (and your guests) by framing the registry as a *suggestion* rather than a requirement. Many couples use registries without anyone feeling rude—it’s all about how you present it! Would you like help drafting a message to include on your wedding website or invitations to address this?

What do you personally think about this — is it right or wrong, and why?

prediction.raw: This is a nuanced situation, and whether you were "AITA" depends on perspective, intent, and context. Here’s a breakdown of the key factors to consider: ### **Arguments That You Were *Not* AITA:** 1. **You Were Being Helpful (and Efficient)** - Many people *do* wait for end credit scenes, especially in superhero movies, and it can cause delays in cleaning theaters. Your intent was to save time for everyone (theaters, staff, and future patrons). - If the theater’s policy is to clean theaters promptly after the main credits, your action aligns with that goal. 2. **It Wasn’t a "Spoiler" in the Traditional Sense** - Unlike plot twists or major reveals, the absence of an end credit scene is a **technical detail**, not a narrative spoiler. It’s not like you ruined a surprise ending—you just clarified a common expectation. 3. **You Were Following Theater Protocol** - Your manager later admitted the flashlight part was false, but the core issue was efficiency. If the theater’s policy is to clean theaters quickly, your action was reasonable. 4. **The Couple’s Reaction Was Overblown** - Some people *do* get upset over minor inconveniences (like waiting for end credits), especially if they’re emotionally invested in the movie. Their reaction might have been more about frustration than actual harm. --- ### **Arguments That You *Could* Be Seen as Rude (or Unnecessary):** 1. **It’s a Minor Inconvenience, Not a Big Deal** - End credit scenes are often short (1-3 minutes). Waiting for them is a small sacrifice for a few extra moments of immersion. Many people don’t even notice if they’re not expecting it. 2. **Some People Enjoy the Ritual** - For some fans, the end credit scene is part of the experience—it’s a way to linger in the movie’s world. Interrupting that can feel like a violation of their enjoyment. 3. **You Might Have Assumed Too Much** - You assumed the couple *wanted* to leave immediately, but they might have been waiting for a reason (e.g., a post-credits scene, a joke, or just habit). Without asking, you interrupted their experience. 4. **Theater Policy Might Be Different** - If the theater *does* have a policy of waiting for end credits (even if it’s not strictly enforced), your action could be seen as bypassing that. --- ### **Was This a "Weird Couple"?** **Probably.** While some people *do* get upset over this, most would either: - Not notice if they weren’t expecting it. - Accept it as a minor inconvenience. - Appreciate the efficiency (especially if they’re in a hurry). The fact that they escalated to a manager suggests they were unusually sensitive to this detail—or possibly just having a bad day. That said, **your manager’s response (giving them a free pass) implies they took the complaint seriously**, which might mean the theater has a policy against interrupting patrons this way. --- ### **Final Verdict: AITA?** **It depends on the theater’s policy and intent, but leaning toward *not AITA* in this case.** - If the goal was **efficiency** and you were following theater protocol, it was reasonable. - If the goal was **being a know-it-all**, then yes, it could be seen as rude. - **The real issue?** The couple’s reaction was disproportionate, but theaters often err on the side of patron comfort over efficiency. **What You Could Do Next:** - If you want to avoid similar situations, you could **ask patrons if they’re waiting for end credits** before telling them to leave. (Example: *"Hey, just a heads-up—no end credit scene here, but if you want to wait, that’s fine!"*) - If the theater *does* have a policy of waiting for end credits, you should follow it—even if it means slower cleaning. **Bottom Line:** You weren’t *wrong* for being efficient, but you could have handled it more diplomatically. The couple was likely overreacting, but theaters often prioritize patron comfort over minor time savings. **Score: 1 (Mostly Not AITA, but could have been smoother)**
